docs.title: Provider Datalab
docs.text:
Declare a team's users, virtual Kubernetes clusters, databases, and sessions in one Datalab resource. The platform supplies identity, storage, and network settings through an EnvironmentConfig.

Platform operators start with Installation. For team workflows, see Virtual clusters and Use a Datalab. The API reference describes resource fields and status.

docs.title: ADR-001: Use Datalab as the Public Contract
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
Implemented.

Users create a Datalab. Provider Datalab turns it into a working data workspace and reports session information on the same resource.

Educates is the first implementation of runtime sessions. It provides the browser editor and terminal. Its resources are created and managed internally.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
A data workspace needs many things: an editor, a terminal, persistent files, credentials, networking, and optional services. Exposing every resource needed to build that workspace would give users a complicated and fragile API.

We need one stable contract that describes what a user wants, while allowing the implementation behind it to change.

docs.title: Make Datalab the only public workspace resource
docs.text:
Users and GitOps tools work with the namespaced Datalab resource. It describes the desired workspace, including its named sessions and optional capabilities.

The Datalab name, namespace, and UID form its stable identity. Generated Pod, Secret, and runtime-resource names are not part of the public contract.

docs.title: Keep the runtime implementation internal
docs.text:
The internal runtime provides the editor, terminal, workspace Pod, sessions, and optional applications. Crossplane translates a Datalab into the runtime and Kubernetes resources required to run it.

This translation is an implementation detail:

User or GitOps tool
  -> Datalab
     -> Provider Datalab reconciliation
        -> internal runtime resources
           -> working Datalab session

Clients never create, update, discover, or depend on runtime resources directly. Crossplane owns those generated resources. This keeps one source of truth and lets the runtime implementation evolve without changing how users manage a Datalab.

The same rule applies if the internal runtime changes later. Runtime resources remain projections of the Datalab and do not become a second public workspace API.

docs.title: Keep user choices separate from operator policy
docs.text:
The Datalab spec contains choices that a user is allowed to make. The operator-owned EnvironmentConfig contains platform settings such as ingress, Keycloak realm, storage classes, security defaults, and extension packages.

Crossplane combines both sets of input. Users therefore get a small API, while operators keep control of security and infrastructure policy.

docs.title: Manage sessions through the Datalab
docs.text:
Each session has a unique name and a desired state such as started or stopped. Provider Datalab creates the internal runtime for started sessions and reports the observed phase, message, and browser URL in Datalab.status.sessions. A stopped session keeps its workspace PVC.

Clients read the Datalab status. They do not look up the internal runtime. Diagnostic phase and message text is not a stable machine-readable lifecycle API.

docs.title: Keep credentials out of the API
docs.text:
Credentials are read from referenced Kubernetes Secrets and copied only where the runtime needs them. Secret values never belong in the Datalab spec, status, logs, or normal client output.

Credentials and security settings currently apply to the whole Datalab. Use separate Datalabs when workloads need different membership or trust boundaries.

docs.title: Add tools without changing the contract
docs.text: Operators can add runtime tools through extension packages. This keeps the Datalab API stable and avoids putting every tool in one large base image.

docs.title: Why This Design
docs.text: Design choice Reason One Datalab API Users have one clear object to create, review, and manage. Runtime stays internal Clients are not coupled to runtime-specific resources or names. Crossplane owns generated resources Reconciliation has one owner and does not compete with user changes. User input and operator policy are separate Self-service does not bypass platform security or infrastructure rules. Status is copied to the Datalab Clients do not need broad access to internal resources. Credentials stay in Secrets The public API does not become a credential-delivery channel.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Provider Datalab is self-contained: clients need only the Datalab API.
  • Changing the internal runtime does not require a second public workspace model.
  • Crossplane remains responsible for generated-resource ownership and cleanup.
  • Operators must validate user-selectable Secret references and other policy-sensitive options.
  • Render tests check generated resources; live tests must also check session transitions and access to services.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Teams need relational databases, document databases, and key-value stores for their applications and data work. They need to request these capabilities without deploying database servers or maintaining backup jobs themselves.

The platform operator needs control over storage, access, maintenance, and recovery. A common service API lets users work independently within those controls and lets the operator provide defined service guarantees.

docs.title: Offer services through Datalab
docs.text:
Use the Datalab API to request these managed services:

Capability Service Datalab field Relational database with SQL and transactions PostgreSQL spec.databases Document database MongoDB spec.documentStores Key-value store and cache Redis spec.cacheStores

Crossplane creates the service resources. The installed database operators manage their workloads. Services belong to the Datalab and continue to run when an interactive session stops. status.connections reports their endpoints and credential Secret references.

docs.title: Keep user configuration small
docs.text:
Users select a service, name it, and set its data storage size. For PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis, they can also set backupStorage to enable backups and size a separate backup volume:

spec:
  databases:
    pg0:
      names:
      - app
      storage: 10Gi
      backupStorage: 30Gi
  documentStores:
    documents:
      storage: 10Gi
      backupStorage: 30Gi
  cacheStores:
    cache:
      storage: 1Gi
      backupStorage: 3Gi

A positive backupStorage enables PostgreSQL, MongoDB, or Redis backups. Zero or an omitted value disables them. PostgreSQL uses pgBackRest; MongoDB uses a composition-managed dump job. Redis uses a composition-managed RDB snapshot job. A data volume alone is not a backup. The backup guide defines the current schedules, retention, and recovery limits.

Users configure the Datalab resource. Crossplane owns the generated resources and can replace manual changes during reconciliation.

docs.title: Assign service operations to the platform operator
docs.text:
Users own their application data, schemas, queries, and requested capacity. The platform operator owns service deployment, supported configurations, upgrades, storage classes, access controls, and operational support. Operator settings come from the platform's EnvironmentConfig.

For enabled backups, the operator must monitor failures and available space, test restores, and provide a recovery procedure. Users do not need to manage backup tools or database operator resources.

docs.title: Define the guarantees for each offered service
docs.text:
The operator must define the supported availability, backup retention, acceptable data loss, recovery time, and data deletion rules. These guarantees depend on the deployed service, storage, and tested recovery procedure. Setting a backup volume size alone does not establish them.

The service API provides consistent provisioning, persistent storage, and connection settings. High availability, recovery after loss of the cluster, and backup retention after Datalab deletion need separate operator provisions.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Users can request common data services and backups through one resource, without a separate database deployment or backup workflow.
  • The platform operator has clear responsibility for operations and the guarantees offered to users.
  • Service data is independent of session state. Its retention still depends on Datalab deletion and storage reclaim rules.
  • Users select from supported service settings. Other database products or configurations need a separate platform decision.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The simple pattern is to use a service account with ws_api. Each Datalab has a Keycloak client with the same name and its own service account. This is enough for services that accept ws_api. That role does not give access to a virtual cluster. Some tasks need more permissions, such as writing data in one virtual namespace. For those tasks, we let a user delegate part of their access through token exchange. The request selects an OAuth scope, and the new token keeps the user's identity with fewer roles.

Selecting one scope does not always exclude the user's other roles. Keycloak includes user-held roles owned by the requesting client, even with Full Scope Allowed off.

docs.title: Separate role definitions from role assignments
docs.text:
Consider a Datalab named s-joe, with two virtual clusters and these roles defined under its Keycloak client:

s-joe
  ws_api
  ws_access
  ws_admin
  vcluster_vc0_cluster-admin
  vcluster_vc0_namespace-demo
  vcluster_vc1_cluster-admin
  vcluster_vc1_namespace-other

This list defines the roles that belong to the client. Role assignments say who holds them. The service account holds only ws_api. Joe, a Datalab administrator, holds all seven through the Datalab users and administrator groups. A regular member holds ws_access, ws_api, and the two additional namespace roles, without the built-in administrator roles.

In a client-credentials request, the service account is the token's subject. In a user-token exchange, Joe is the subject. The Datalab client authenticates the exchange request, but its service account's role list does not limit Joe's roles.

docs.title: The broad role mapper breaks downscoping
docs.text:
Suppose Joe asks a service to write data in namespace demo of vc0. The service exchanges his access token with these parameters and the existing Datalab client credentials:

grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
subject_token=<Joe's access token>
scope=s-joe:vclusters_vc0_namespace-demo
audience=s-joe

The intended result contains ws_api and vcluster_vc0_namespace-demo.

Keycloak includes roles that the subject holds under the requesting client, even when Full Scope Allowed is off. A broad Client Roles mapper then writes all of those roles into resource_access.s-joe.roles. In this example, that means all seven roles above, including administration of both virtual clusters. The optional namespace scope does not filter them out.

Joe has not gained a new permission. The service that receives his exchanged token has received more access than this task needs. It can use his virtual cluster administrator roles even though the request selected one namespace. Keeping ws_api is expected; keeping those unrequested roles defeats the purpose of the exchange.

This behavior comes from Keycloak's role selection. It is not an extra grant made by the test or the Datalab service account.

docs.title: Select the emitted roles explicitly
docs.text:
The Datalab client uses basic, profile, and email as identity-only default scopes. Each additional vcluster profile has an optional scope, so the caller must request it explicitly.

Each profile scope uses Keycloak's built-in Role Name mapper to select its one role, but only when the user holds that role. A dedicated mapper selects ws_api under the same rule. These mappers put the selected roles into a temporary role set for the current request. A built-in Realm Roles mapper writes that set into resource_access.<datalab>.roles. This creates no stored realm roles or new user assignments. It needs no script or custom Keycloak plugin.

Joe's namespace request then produces:

sub: <Joe's user ID>
aud: [s-joe]
resource_access:
  s-joe:
    roles:
    - ws_api
    - vcluster_vc0_namespace-demo

The token cannot carry Joe's administrator roles or the other namespace profile unless the selected scopes permit them. A user without the requested profile role receives no such role; the service must check the result before using it. A hardcoded claim would not make that check against the user's assignments.

docs.title: Keep interactive roles out of exchanged tokens
docs.text: The separate optional s-joe:interactive scope supplies Datalab and built-in administrator roles for direct browser login. A client policy rejects this scope during token exchange, including requests that mix it with a namespace scope. Otherwise, a caller could request it and defeat the restriction.

docs.title: Enable exchange only after its controls are ready
docs.text:
Each Datalab client enables exchange automatically after its scopes, mappers, and policy are ready. There is no platform opt-in setting. Crossplane Usage resources keep a policy's scope and profile until the policy has been deleted.

Keycloak 26.2 or later is required. Default identity scopes must contain no role grants or role mappers.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A service can receive a token for one configured profile while the user keeps their wider Datalab permissions. The user's identity stays in the token.
  • The platform must provide identity-only default scopes. A service account with ws_api alone cannot access a virtual cluster.
  • Render tests check configuration. Live tests must inspect issued user tokens and use them against the virtual API. Namespace access must work, cluster access must fail, unassigned roles must stay absent, and exchange with the interactive scope must fail.
  • Selecting a kubeconfig profile alone does not reduce a token's permissions.

docs.title: Additional services
docs.text:
Run services such as Dask or MLflow as Kubernetes workloads from your Datalab terminal. These examples need Kubernetes API access and permission to create Pods, Deployments, Services, and PVCs in the target namespace. If the Datalab has no session, declare one first.

Use a vCluster for tools that need their own CRDs, controllers, or cluster roles. For a short-lived process, you can run it in the terminal and use the editor's Ports tab to open its web interface.

Use the Datalab service fields for managed PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis stores. The environment also supplies a shared OCI registry.

docs.title: Dask
docs.text:
Dask runs tasks across a scheduler and workers. This example creates one scheduler and one worker in the current namespace. Connect to the scheduler from Python with dask.distributed.Client.

kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: dask-scheduler
spec:
  selector:
    app: dask-scheduler
  ports:
    - name: tcp-scheduler
      port: 8786
      targetPort: 8786
    - name: http-dashboard
      port: 8787
      targetPort: 8787
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: dask-scheduler
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: dask-scheduler
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: dask-scheduler
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: scheduler
          image: daskdev/dask:2025.4.0
          args: ["dask-scheduler", "--dashboard-address", ":8787"]
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8786
            - containerPort: 8787
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: "500m", memory: "1Gi"}
            limits:   {cpu: "1",    memory: "2Gi"}
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: dask-worker
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: dask-worker
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: dask-worker
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: daskdev/dask:2025.4.0
          args: ["dask-worker", "tcp://dask-scheduler:8786", "--nthreads", "2", "--memory-limit", "2GB"]
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: "500m", memory: "1Gi"}
            limits:   {cpu: "1",    memory: "2Gi"}
EOF

Open the scheduler dashboard through the editor's Ports tab:

kubectl port-forward svc/dask-scheduler 8787:8787

Dask Gateway also needs cluster-wide resources. Use a vCluster or ask the operator to install it. With the dask Helm repository configured, run:

helm repo update
helm upgrade --install dask-gateway dask/dask-gateway \
  -n "${DEFAULT_NAMESPACE:-default}" \
  --create-namespace \
  --set gateway.auth.type=simple \
  --set gateway.auth.simple.password='' \
  --set traefik.service.type=ClusterIP \
  --set gateway.backend.image.name=ghcr.io/dask/dask-gateway \
  --set gateway.backend.image.tag=2025.4.0 \
  --wait --atomic

docs.title: MLflow
docs.text:
MLflow records experiment runs and their artifacts. This example stores its SQLite database on a PVC and artifacts in an existing S3 bucket. Set BUCKET to a bucket your Datalab can write to.

The PVC belongs to the current namespace. Check namespace deletion rules and the volume's reclaim policy before storing records you need to keep. For a shared service, use a managed database and arrange artifact backups with the operator.

export BUCKET=s-jeff # Use a bucket your Datalab can write to.

kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: minio-creds
type: Opaque
stringData:
  accessKey: "${AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}"
  secretKey: "${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}"
  sessionToken: "${AWS_SESSION_TOKEN:-}"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: minio-config
data:
  endpoint: "${AWS_ENDPOINT_URL}"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: mlflow
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: mlflow
spec:
  selector:
    app: mlflow
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 5000
      targetPort: 5000
      protocol: TCP
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: mlflow
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: mlflow
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: mlflow
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: mlflow
          image: ghcr.io/mlflow/mlflow:v3.14.0
          command: ["/bin/sh","-lc"]
          args:
            - |
              python -m pip install --no-cache-dir --upgrade pip &&
              pip install --no-cache-dir boto3 &&
              exec mlflow server \
                --backend-store-uri sqlite:////mlflow/mlflow.db \
                --serve-artifacts \
                --artifacts-destination s3://"${BUCKET}"/mlruns \
                --host 0.0.0.0 --port 5000 \
                --workers 2 \
                --allowed-hosts '*' \
                --cors-allowed-origins '*'
          ports:
            - containerPort: 5000
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "100m", memory: "512Mi" }
            limits:   { cpu: "300m", memory: "2Gi" }
          env:
            - name: MLFLOW_S3_ENDPOINT_URL
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef: { name: minio-config, key: endpoint }
            - name: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef: { name: minio-creds, key: accessKey }
            - name: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef: { name: minio-creds, key: secretKey }
            - name: AWS_SESSION_TOKEN
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef: { name: minio-creds, key: sessionToken }
            - name: AWS_S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE
              value: "true"
            - name: AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED
              value: "true"
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /mlflow
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: "/", port: 5000 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: "/", port: 5000 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 20
            periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: mlflow
EOF

Open the MLflow interface through the editor's Ports tab:

kubectl port-forward svc/mlflow 5000:5000

Point your code at the forwarded tracking server:

export MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI="http://127.0.0.1:5000"

docs.title: PostgreSQL with psql
docs.text:
The Jeff example provides POSTGRES_PG0_DEV_URL for database dev on pg0. Run this command from a session with that variable to start a psql Pod in the current namespace:

envsubst '${POSTGRES_PG0_DEV_URL}' <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pgsql-debug
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: psql
    image: postgres:17
    stdin: true
    tty: true
    command:
      - sh
      - -lc
      - |
        exec psql "$POSTGRES_URL"
    env:
      - name: POSTGRES_URL
        value: ${POSTGRES_PG0_DEV_URL}
EOF

Attach to the Pod after it starts:

kubectl attach -it pgsql-debug

Check the connection with a temporary table:

\set ON_ERROR_STOP on
CREATE TEMP TABLE datalab_check (value text);
INSERT INTO datalab_check VALUES ('ready');
SELECT value FROM datalab_check;

docs.title: Keep or remove a service
docs.text: Remove test services when the experiment ends. Before keeping one, agree with the platform team on its storage, backups, monitoring, upgrades, and deletion. Back up the service data separately from the session volume.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Each Datalab has one confidential Keycloak client with the same name. For example, the Datalab s-joe has a client named s-joe and its own service account. Use that client for browser login, CLI device login, machine access, and restricted user-token exchange. The same client credentials and Secret references serve these flows.

Use Keycloak 26.2 or later with Standard Token Exchange V2 and client policies enabled. Default scopes must not add the unrestricted client-role mapper. Enable the grant-type, client-scopes, and reject-request client-policy providers and the built-in Role Name and Realm Roles protocol mappers.

docs.title: Groups and roles
docs.text:
Users in spec.users must exist in the configured realm. The first user and users with userOverrides.<user>.role: admin belong to the administrator group. All listed users belong to the Datalab users group.

Managed group or account Assigned Datalab client roles <datalab> ws_access, ws_api, all explicitly configured additional vcluster profiles <datalab>-admin ws_admin, ws_api, all additional profiles, each instance's built-in cluster-admin role Datalab service account ws_api only

Administrators also inherit the users group's grants. The provider replaces managed group grants on each reconciliation. Profile removal or rename removes its grants. Direct user assignments are unchanged.

Only spec.vclusters.<instance>.groups defines selectable exchange profiles. The reserved cluster-admin entry never adds an exchange scope, even when explicitly declared. Empty groups give regular members no vcluster roles; administrators retain each declared instance's built-in admin role and profile. Role names remain vcluster_<instance>_<group>.

docs.title: OAuth scopes and direct login
docs.text:
The Datalab client's dedicated role mapping permits only ws_api. It appears in a token only if its subject holds that role. Default scopes are basic, profile, and email; keep these scopes free of role grants and role mappers. Keycloak includes a client's own roles even with Full Scope Allowed off. The provider therefore uses Role Name mappers to select held roles for each request, then a Realm Roles mapper to write that temporary role set under resource_access.<datalab>.roles. This creates no realm roles or user grants. For the reason and a worked example, see Token exchange for downscoping.

Optional OAuth scope Permitted roles <datalab>:vclusters_<instance>_<group> Exactly vcluster_<instance>_<group> for an additional configured profile <datalab>:interactive ws_access, ws_admin, and each instance's built-in cluster-admin role

Scopes permit only roles that the subject holds. They are never realm-default scopes. Scope names differ from role names: bare ws_admin or vcluster_vc0_namespace-demo are not generated OAuth scopes.

A direct authorization-code request to s-joe can use these parameters:

client_id=s-joe
response_type=code
redirect_uri=http://localhost:8080/callback
scope=openid profile email s-joe:interactive s-joe:vclusters_vc0_namespace-demo

Use the normal state and PKCE checks, then authenticate the confidential client when redeeming the code. Request only the scopes needed by the application. For a namespace-only direct login, omit s-joe:interactive.

You can also use a separate login client in the same realm. Its scope mappings control the roles in its tokens. Before exchanging one of those tokens through the Datalab client, check that it contains the Datalab audience and the requested roles. Configure those claims on the separate login client.

docs.title: CLI device login
docs.text:
The provider enables Device Authorization Grant on the existing confidential client. The built-in cluster-admin kubeconfig helper uses this flow with a separate client secret. It requests openid offline_access <datalab>:interactive, prints a verification URL and user code to stderr, and waits for the user to approve the login in a browser. No localhost callback is needed.

The resulting access token represents the user who signs in. Only that user's assigned roles can appear. Possession of the client secret does not grant cluster-admin. The service account remains assigned only ws_api; the helper does not use grant_type=client_credentials.

The helper reuses cached tokens and attempts refresh before starting a new login. A valid cached token needs no client secret. Login and refresh require the secret through a private file or a hidden terminal prompt. See human access for commands and cache settings. Additional profiles use a caller-supplied access token and do not start login.

docs.title: Login lifetime
docs.text:
Keycloak sets these lifetimes; the helper uses the issued expiry values.

Lifetime Setting Time to approve a device code Realm oauth2DeviceCodeLifespan Access token validity Access Token Lifespan CLI offline session validity Offline Session Idle/Max and Client Offline Session Idle/Max

For the CLI cache duration, offline session limits, and revocation, see human login lifetime.

docs.title: User-token exchange
docs.text:
Each Datalab client enables exchange automatically after its scopes, mappers, and policy are ready. No extra setting is required.

Standard Token Exchange V2 uses the existing Datalab client credentials. The caller's access token remains the subject; exchange does not use the service account's permissions. A managed client policy combines the grant-type and client-scopes conditions with reject-request. It rejects <datalab>:interactive during token exchange, including requests that combine it with allowed profile scopes. Direct interactive login can still use it.

Send this form to the configured realm's token endpoint. Authenticate with the existing confidential s-joe client through the approved credential path. The placeholder below represents the original caller access token.

grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
subject_token=<caller access token>
subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token
requested_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token
scope=s-joe:vclusters_vc0_namespace-demo
audience=s-joe

The caller token must contain s-joe in aud, unless it was issued to s-joe itself. Keycloak uses this check to confirm that the token was intended for the Datalab client. The Datalab audience is always available in tokens issued by that client. The audience parameter filters available audiences; it does not add missing mappings.

For an eligible caller, the required authorization claims are:

iss: https://identity.acme.com/realms/acme
sub: <same user subject as the caller token>
aud: [s-joe]
resource_access:
  s-joe:
    roles: [ws_api, vcluster_vc0_namespace-demo]

This applies to both members and administrators selecting the profile. The result must omit ws_access, ws_admin, built-in cluster-admin, unrequested profiles, and roles for other Datalabs. Identity claims can remain.

To use tokens issued by the Datalab client with another service, add its client ID to EnvironmentConfig.data.iam.extraAudiences. For example, for EOEPCA Workspace API:

iam:
  extraAudiences:
  - workspace-api

An exchange request can then include both audience=s-joe and audience=workspace-api to retain those two recipients. Removing the setting removes its managed audience mapper. For tokens issued by a separate login client, configure the Datalab audience on that client.

Keycloak checks the user's role grants before applying an optional profile scope. A user without the role can receive a successful response with that scope and role omitted. Consumers must reject a result missing a requested role. This is the documented server behavior; actual issuance must be checked against the deployed server. Render checks do not prove token contents. See Keycloak scope permissions.

Reconciliation removes a deleted or renamed profile's optional association, role scope mapping, Client Scope, and managed group grants. Instance deletion removes its profiles too. Already-issued JWTs can retain their claims until expiry. Downloading a kubeconfig profile neither grants permissions nor reduces a supplied token's permissions. For delegated access, exchange the token first, then give the recipient the profile and returned access token. The additional profile helper reads that token from a file and needs no client secret. The virtual API still checks the realm issuer, Datalab audience, signature, validity, and configured Datalab roles. Its username is sub; groups are datalab:<datalab>:<role>. Existing virtual RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding rules apply without an authentication change.

docs.title: Credential Secrets and machine access
docs.text:
Secret Namespace Use <datalab>-oauth-client Claim namespace Source credentials for the existing Datalab client <datalab>-oauth2-client Runtime namespace Created only for public Data/S3 OAuth2 proxies; contains client_id, client_secret, and cookie_secret

The runtime copy is needed only when Data is enabled and exposed through an Ingress or HTTPRoute. It is created after the runtime namespace is known and removed when that proxy is disabled. Token exchange and virtual-cluster access do not need this copy. The aggregate session Secret includes OAuth fields delivered to sessions.

Anyone with the client secret can request a service-account token. Grant read access only to authorized callers. With grant_type=client_credentials and no optional scopes, the Datalab service account receives only ws_api.

Virtual API profile Secrets contain public settings and no credentials. See virtual API access for credential files. Permission to download a profile is separate from permission to read service credentials.

docs.title: Exchange caller checks
docs.text:
A service that exchanges tokens for users must:

  • Accept full profile scope names, or translate short names with the Datalab name.
  • Allow only currently configured additional profiles and check each requested role against the caller's validated token.
  • Retain the original caller access token for subject_token and authenticate exchange with the existing Datalab client credentials.
  • Validate the returned signature, validity, issuer, exact audiences, user subject, requested roles, and absence of unexpected authorization permissions.
  • Reject missing requested roles even when the token endpoint returns success.
  • Check that the caller is allowed to request token issuance through that service, in addition to the token and role checks above.

docs.title: OAuth2 discovery
docs.text:
The provider publishes the existing client in status.oauth2, separately from service connections:

status:
  oauth2:
  - name: s-joe
    type: client
    issuerUrl: https://identity.acme.com/realms/acme
    secretRef:
      name: s-joe-oauth-client
      namespace: workspace
    ready: true

name is the actual OAuth2 client ID, not Keycloak's internal UUID. Names are unique and type is always client. Entries contain only metadata and Secret references; credentials stay in the referenced Secret.

Readiness requires the observed client and credential Secret to be ready, with matching client credentials. Removed sources clear stale entries. Discovery does not grant permission to read a Secret or authorize a service request.

docs.title: Session ingress
docs.text: Configure sign-in before users start a session. The examples use Kyverno to configure NGINX or APISIX session Ingress objects.

docs.title: Set the shared ingress settings
docs.text:
Set the ingress class, domain, and TLS Secret in the EnvironmentConfig. Use the same values in the session runtime installation, for example:

clusterIngressDomain: lab.acme.com
clusterIngressClass: apisix
tlsCertificateRef:
  name: wildcard-tls
  namespace: workspace

Use a wildcard certificate for *.lab.acme.com.

docs.title: Generated session resources
docs.text:
For a Datalab named s-jane with a default session, set ingress.domain to lab.acme.com. The session ingress hosts include:

s-jane-default.lab.acme.com
editor-s-jane-default.lab.acme.com
s-jane-default-editor.lab.acme.com
data-s-jane-default.lab.acme.com
s-jane-default-data.lab.acme.com

The generated ingresses carry labels that are suitable for platform policy:

training.educates.dev/application: workshop
training.educates.dev/component: session
training.educates.dev/environment.name: s-jane

For s-jane, the generated client includes redirect and web-origin entries for the Datalab root and each declared session host:

https://s-jane.lab.acme.com/*
https://s-jane-default.lab.acme.com/*
https://editor-s-jane-default.lab.acme.com/*
https://s-jane-default-editor.lab.acme.com/*
https://data-s-jane-default.lab.acme.com/*
https://s-jane-default-data.lab.acme.com/*
http://localhost:*

A service that belongs to s-jane can use this client. Shared browser ingress can use a central platform client and check the generated Datalab roles.

docs.title: Apply ingress policy
docs.text: Apply controller settings through platform policy so they cover every session Ingress. The examples use Kyverno CEL policies. They need CRDs that serve MutatingPolicy and GeneratingPolicy in policies.kyverno.io/v1. Kyverno is required for these policies, not for Provider Datalab itself. Adapt the domains, issuer, and controller settings in the linked manifests.

docs.title: NGINX Ingress with OAuth2 Proxy
docs.text:
Run OAuth2 Proxy as a shared service with its own OAuth client. Use a redirect URI such as https://auth.lab.acme.com/oauth2/callback. Its authorization policy must check access to the Datalab named in the requested host.

Apply the NGINX policy to add external-auth annotations to matching session Ingress objects. Set the proxy cookie domain to cover the session hosts, for example .lab.acme.com, and allow redirects only to that domain.

docs.title: APISIX Ingress configured by Kyverno
docs.text:
The APISIX manifest gives Kyverno permission to create ApisixPluginConfig resources, generates one in each session namespace, and attaches it to matching Ingress objects. APISIX checks incoming requests; Kyverno configures the resources.

The example uses openid-connect with a central public client named datalab-sessions. Its opa entry points to an external OPA service. The manifest does not deploy that service or supply its policy. Configure both for your platform so that the authorizer checks access to the requested Datalab. OPA is needed only for this example.

The policies do not read Secrets. For a confidential central client, use the ingress controller's supported Secret mechanism to supply its credential.

The plugin forwards the access token in Authorization and disables ID token, userinfo, and refresh token forwarding. Check that your authorizer and upstream service accept these settings.

Kyverno generates the plugin's session secret once. Synchronization is disabled to keep it stable. After changing the template, recreate an existing generated plugin config or restart its session to apply the change.

For another ingress controller, match session Ingress objects by label and domain, then attach its authentication and authorization settings.

docs.title: Install Provider Datalab
docs.text: Run these commands from a repository checkout with access to the target cluster. For a shared installation, manage manifests and Secrets through your platform's GitOps and Secret tools.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The cluster needs Crossplane, the Educates session runtime, an ingress controller, Keycloak, and an S3-compatible object store. The CNI must enforce Kubernetes NetworkPolicy. Use Crossplane from the supported range in the package's metadata.

Install the session runtime with its CRDs and controller RBAC before creating Datalabs. Follow the runtime installation guide. The runtime ingress class, domain, and TLS Secret must match the settings below.

Install the operators for the managed stores you plan to offer. Provider Datalab integration tests use these versions:

Datalab field Operator Test version Required resource API spec.databases Crunchy PostgreSQL Operator (PGO) 6.0.2 PostgresCluster in postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/v1 spec.documentStores MongoDB Kubernetes Operator 1.14.0 MongoDBCommunity in mongodbcommunity.mongodb.com/v1 spec.cacheStores Opstree Redis Operator 0.27.0 (Helm chart 0.27.0) Redis in redis.redis.opstreelabs.in/v1beta2

These are fixed test pins. Other versions need validation before use.

Install each operator's CRDs before its controller. The integration harness shows the tested installation settings. Backup volumes need a StorageClass that supports ReadWriteOnce; see backup settings.

Gateway exposure also needs a Gateway API controller. Data uses HTTPRoute with HTTP and TLS-terminating HTTPS listeners. External PostgreSQL access uses TLSRoute in gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 and direct TLS with SNI.

For spec.vclusters, apply the supplied provider RBAC and configure an HTTPS issuer, allowed StorageClasses, and an HTTPS Gateway listener. The host needs ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and BackendTLSPolicy support. See virtual cluster setup.

docs.title: 1. Choose the claim namespace
docs.text:
This guide uses workspace for Datalab resources and their namespaced ProviderConfigs:

kubectl create namespace workspace
kubectl create namespace datalab

Input storage Secrets live in datalab, as set by storage.secretNamespace in the environment examples. Each Datalab also has a separate namespace for its runtime and shared services.

docs.title: 2. Install provider dependencies
docs.text:
Apply the files in dependencies/ in this order:

File Purpose 00-mrap.yaml Activate the managed resource kinds used by the composition. 01-deploymentRuntimeConfigs.yaml Set provider and function Pod security. 02-providers.yaml Install the Kubernetes, Helm, and Keycloak providers. 03-providerConfigs.yaml Configure those providers in the claim namespace. functions.yaml Install the composition functions. rbac.yaml Grant provider-kubernetes access to the resources it manages.

Apply 03-providerConfigs.yaml with kubectl apply -n workspace -f .... Create its referenced Keycloak credential Secret in that namespace through your platform's Secret tools. The Keycloak account needs permission to manage clients, client scopes, service-account roles, groups, memberships, role mappings, and client policies in the target realm.

Use Keycloak 26.2 or later. Configure identity scopes, client policies, and browser sign-in as described in Authentication. The realm must permit the built-in offline_access scope and user role for CLI device login.

Use the package pins in the dependency manifests. Wait for the provider and function revisions to report healthy before installing the configuration package. The provider-kubernetes RBAC includes access to Pods for readiness checks and PVCs for session storage.

docs.title: 3. Install the configuration package
docs.text:
Save this resource as configuration.yaml. Replace 0.12.0-rc.8 with the release tag you want to install.

apiVersion: pkg.crossplane.io/v1
kind: Configuration
metadata:
  name: datalab
spec:
  package: ghcr.io/versioneer-tech/provider-datalab:0.12.0-rc.8
  skipDependencyResolution: true

Apply it and check the package conditions:

kubectl apply -f configuration.yaml
kubectl get configurations.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get configurationrevisions.pkg.crossplane.io

The package installs the Datalab resource definition and composition. Its providers and functions are managed separately by the platform.

For a source installation, apply xrd.yaml before composition.yaml so Kubernetes retains the OAuth2 discovery fields.

The manifest build guide explains how to change the pipeline response TTL before building a package.

docs.title: 4. Set the shared environment
docs.text:
Create an EnvironmentConfig named datalab with values for your cluster. This example uses NGINX Ingress for Data and the registry:

apiVersion: apiextensions.crossplane.io/v1beta1
kind: EnvironmentConfig
metadata:
  name: datalab
data:
  iam:
    realm: acme
    issuerURL: https://identity.acme.com/realms/acme
    internalURL: http://keycloak.keycloak:8080/realms/acme
  ingress:
    enabled: true
    class: nginx
    domain: lab.acme.com
    secret: wildcard-tls
    annotations:
      nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "0"
      nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-request-buffering: "off"
      nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffering: "off"
      nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "3600"
      nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-send-timeout: "3600"
  oauth2Proxy:
    upstreamTimeout: 3600s
  storage:
    endpoint: https://s3.acme.com
    provider: Other
    region: us-east-1
    forcePathStyle: "true"
    secretNamespace: datalab
    type: s3
  storageClasses:
    allowed:
    - sbs-default
    - sbs-default-retain
  network:
    externalEgressCIDRs:
    - 0.0.0.0/0
    - ::/0
    serviceCIDR: "10.43.0.0/16"
    podCIDRs:
    - 10.42.0.0/16
    blacklistIPs:
    - 169.254.169.254/32
    - fd00:ec2::254/128
    - 169.254.42.42/32
    - fd00:42::42/128
    excludePolicies: []
  defaults:
    vcluster:
      enabled: true
    registry:
      enabled: true
    data:
      enabled: true
      readOnlyMount: false
    overallQuota:
      storage: 100Gi
    security:
      externalEgress: true

Replace the example storage classes, network ranges, and DNS names before applying it. Configure authentication before users start sessions.

docs.title: Service addresses
docs.text:
Enable either ingress.enabled or httpRoute.enabled for public service access. Using both stops reconciliation. On each Datalab's hostname, /v2/ serves the registry and other paths serve Data. Virtual API routes use their instance path, such as /.vc0. With httpRoute.enableS3, requests signed by S3 clients use the read-only S3 service on the same host.

With neither exposure method enabled, Data is available through a session's authenticated ingress. The registry is available only inside the cluster.

For Gateway API exposure, replace the example's ingress.enabled: true with false and add:

data:
  httpRoute:
    enabled: true
    parentName: default
    parentNamespace: contour
    sectionName: workspaces-https
    httpSectionName: workspaces-http
    timeouts:
      request: 3600s
      backendRequest: 3600s

The Gateway needs HTTP and TLS-terminating HTTPS listeners and must accept routes from runtime namespaces. It manages the service certificate. Keep the ingress class and TLS Secret set for the session runtime. For the optional read-only S3 endpoint, see S3 client access.

docs.title: Large file transfers
docs.text:
ingress.annotations applies to both Data and registry Ingress objects. The example permits any upload size, streams requests and responses, and allows one hour between read or write operations. These annotations require the community ingress-nginx controller. Use your controller's settings if you use another implementation. The composition does not add controller-specific annotations.

httpRoute.timeouts applies to Data, read-only S3, and registry backend rules. Both timeouts default to one hour. If only request is set, backendRequest uses that value. A nonzero backend timeout must not exceed a nonzero request timeout. Use 0s for both to disable these deadlines.

Gateway API has no standard body-size or buffering setting. Configure the Gateway controller and any upstream load balancer to allow the required body size, stream transfers, and permit long connections. The controller must support HTTPRoute timeouts.

oauth2Proxy.upstreamTimeout defaults to one hour. It limits the wait for packageR response headers after the request body is sent. It does not limit the time to transfer the request or response body. Use 0s to disable this wait limit.

packageR permits all browser origins (*) for public catalog access. To restrict origins, configure the Gateway to replace or remove backend CORS headers and handle preflight requests. Adding a header does not restrict the wildcard. Cookie-based cross-origin access needs a separate policy.

docs.title: EnvironmentConfig values and defaults
docs.text:
All paths below are relative to EnvironmentConfig.data. Defaults apply when a setting is omitted; example values such as cluster CIDRs, endpoints, and StorageClass names are not built-in defaults.

Select a specific EnvironmentConfig with the datalabs.pkg.internal/environment annotation or label to use its settings without per-Datalab overrides, as shown in the datalab-custom example. The annotation takes priority over the label; the default selection is datalab.

Runtime settings come from the EnvironmentConfig. The XRD retains unknown fields, but extra fields in spec do not override these settings.

docs.title: Runtime and service defaults
docs.text:
Setting Default Use defaults.vcluster.enabled true Virtual Kubernetes API for each started session. defaults.registry.enabled true Shared OCI registry backed by the Datalab S3 bucket. defaults.data.enabled true Shared packageR service and its configured endpoint. defaults.data.readOnlyMount false Read-only application permissions when enabled; storage IAM still applies. defaults.quota.memory 2Gi Session memory request. defaults.quota.storage 1Gi Workspace PVC size. defaults.quota.budget medium Session namespace budget. defaults.overallQuota.storage 100Gi Aggregate PVC request limit in the environment namespace. defaults.security.policy baseline Pod security level: restricted, baseline, or privileged. defaults.security.kubernetesAccess true Session Kubernetes service account token. defaults.security.kubernetesRole edit Session role: view, edit, or admin. defaults.security.externalEgress true Broad egress to the configured external CIDRs. defaults.persistence.storageClassName First allowed class, or cluster default Workspace StorageClass; a value outside the allowlist falls back to its first entry. defaults.files [] Workshop file bundles. packages [] Session extension packages.

Session PVC names and namespaces are listed in status.sessions[].pvcRef. status.sessions[].pvcSize reports the requested size.

File bundles and extension packages are passed to the session runtime unchanged. Set Data enablement before creating Datalabs because the runtime saves each environment's Workshop specification. See file sources for a file bundle example.

docs.title: Service images
docs.text:
Set these image references under data.images in the EnvironmentConfig. Use a full image reference with a tag or digest. Omitted settings use the defaults below.

Setting Default image tag Use images.packageR ghcr.io/versioneer-tech/package-r:vnext.1.1.0 Data server and its database init container. images.registry registry:3.1.2 CNCF Distribution registry. images.rclone rclone/rclone:1.71.0 Data S3 service. Session extension packages are configured separately. images.mongo quay.io/mongodb/mongodb-community-server:8.0.12-ubi8 MongoDB server. The default database version is 8.0.12. images.mongoBackup mongo:8.0.12 MongoDB backup tools. If omitted, its tag follows the database version. images.redis quay.io/opstree/redis:v7.0.15 Redis server and its init container. images.redisBackup redis:7.0.15 Redis backup tools. images.oauth2Proxy quay.io/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy:v7.15.4 OAuth2 Proxy for Data and S3.

The default OAuth2 Proxy image is also pinned by digest in the composition. A MongoDB image tag that starts with major.minor.patch sets the database version. For a digest without a version tag, set documentStore.version to the image's MongoDB version. Use compatible server and backup images.

docs.title: Identity and endpoints
docs.text: Setting Default Use iam.realm default Keycloak realm; users must already exist here. iam.namespace keycloak Namespace selected by IAM egress rules. iam.issuerURL Not set Public OIDC issuer for Data and virtual cluster access. iam.internalURL Not set Token and signing-key URL; required for permanent Data exposure. iam.extraAudiences [] Additional audiences for tokens issued by the Datalab client. The Datalab audience is always included. ingress.enabled false Public Data and registry Ingress. ingress.class Empty Ingress class for sessions and services. ingress.domain default for sessions Public host suffix for sessions and services. ingress.secret wildcard-tls for sessions TLS Secret; must be set for Data Ingress. ingress.annotations {} Annotations on service Ingress objects. httpRoute.enabled false Public Data and registry Gateway routes. httpRoute.enableS3 false Read-only S3 endpoint; requires httpRoute.enabled. httpRoute.parentName Not set Gateway name; required when Gateway exposure is enabled. httpRoute.parentNamespace Not set Gateway namespace; required when Gateway exposure is enabled. httpRoute.sectionName Not set HTTPS listener; required when Gateway exposure is enabled. httpRoute.httpSectionName Not set HTTP redirect listener; required when Data uses Gateway exposure. httpRoute.timeouts.request 3600s Request deadline for Data, S3, and registry routes; 0s disables it. httpRoute.timeouts.backendRequest Request timeout Deadline for each backend request, including its response body. oauth2Proxy.upstreamTimeout 3600s Wait for packageR response headers after sending the request body.

docs.title: Storage and managed stores
docs.text:
Setting Default Use storage.endpoint Empty Endpoint reachable by runtime Pods; the input Secret's AWS_ENDPOINT_URL takes priority. storage.region Empty Object-store region; the input Secret's AWS_REGION takes priority. storage.type Empty rclone backend type, usually s3. storage.provider Empty for rclone; Other for the S3 proxy Object-store provider. storage.forcePathStyle true Path-style S3 requests. storage.secretNamespace Datalab namespace, or default Input storage Secret namespace. storageClasses.allowed [] Allowed workspace StorageClasses; an empty list permits any configured class. vcluster.resources.requests CPU 200m, memory 1Gi, ephemeral storage 1Gi Control-plane requests; supplied fields override these defaults. vcluster.resources.limits CPU 4, memory 4Gi, ephemeral storage 10Gi Control-plane limits; supplied fields override these defaults. vcluster.backingStore.database.embedded enabled: false, extraArgs: [] Native embedded database options, including enabled, dataSource, and extraArgs. vcluster.storage 5Gi Default control-plane PVC size for named virtual clusters. vcluster.storageClasses.allowed Required when virtual clusters are declared Host classes exposed to virtual workloads. vcluster.storageClasses.default First allowed class Virtual workload default class. vcluster.storageClassName Virtual default class Control-plane StorageClass; must be allowed. vcluster.issuerCA System trust PEM CA for the HTTPS issuer. vcluster.discoveryURL Issuer discovery Optional HTTPS discovery address. vcluster.backendTLS.apiVersion gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 BackendTLSPolicy API served by the Gateway. ingress.certificateAuthority System trust PEM Gateway CA embedded in profile kubeconfigs. database.storageClassName Cluster default PostgreSQL data StorageClass. database.backupStorageClassName Cluster default PostgreSQL backup StorageClass. database.tlsRoute.parentName Not set PostgreSQL Gateway name. database.tlsRoute.parentNamespace Not set PostgreSQL Gateway namespace. database.tlsRoute.sectionName Not set PostgreSQL TLS listener. documentStore.version 8.0.12, or version from images.mongo Database version; set it for an image without a version tag. documentStore.storageClassName Cluster default MongoDB data StorageClass. documentStore.backupStorageClassName Cluster default MongoDB backup StorageClass. cacheStore.storageClassName Cluster default Redis data StorageClass. cacheStore.backupStorageClassName Cluster default Redis backup StorageClass.

PostgreSQL TLSRoutes are created only when all three database.tlsRoute settings are present.

docs.title: Network rules
docs.text: Setting Default Use network.externalEgressCIDRs [] External destination ranges; empty means no broad external allow rule. network.blacklistIPs [] CIDRs excluded from external egress. network.podCIDRs [] Host Pod ranges excluded from external egress. network.serviceCIDR Not set Host Service range excluded from external egress. network.excludePolicies [] Generated policies to omit. network.internalEgress [] Explicit cross-namespace destinations. network.internalIngress [] Explicit cross-namespace sources. network.internalEgress[].namespace, network.internalIngress[].namespace Required for each entry Peer namespace. network.internalEgress[].podSelector, network.internalIngress[].podSelector {} Peer Pod selector; omitted means all Pods in the peer namespace. network.internalEgress[].ports, network.internalIngress[].ports [] Ports; omitted means all ports. network.internalEgress[].ports[].port, network.internalIngress[].ports[].port Required for each port entry Named or numbered port. network.internalEgress[].ports[].protocol, network.internalIngress[].ports[].protocol Kubernetes default (TCP) Port protocol. network.internalEgress[].ports[].endPort, network.internalIngress[].ports[].endPort Not set End of a numeric port range. network.internalIngress[].targetPodSelector {} Runtime Pods selected by the ingress policy; omitted means all runtime Pods.

docs.title: Network access
docs.text:
Set network.podCIDRs and network.serviceCIDR to the host cluster's network ranges. They are excluded from broad external egress so that it does not also allow access to other Datalab namespaces. Use the cluster configuration for the Service CIDR. A DNS Service IP alone does not identify the full range. Pod CIDRs can be listed with:

kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"  "}{.spec.podCIDR}{"  "}{.spec.podCIDRs}{"\n"}{end}'

Use 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0 for all external IPv4 and IPv6 destinations, or list narrower ranges in network.externalEgressCIDRs.

For a backend Pod in another namespace, add an internalEgress entry:

network:
  internalEgress:
  - namespace: minio
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        v1.min.io/tenant: default
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 9000

Use network.internalIngress for inbound traffic. It uses the same fields as internalEgress, with namespace and podSelector selecting the source:

network:
  internalIngress:
  - namespace: operations
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus
    targetPodSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: package-r
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8888

These rules apply to existing runtime namespaces too. See Network policies for how policies combine, Data access, and policy exclusions.

docs.title: 5. Supply storage credentials
docs.text:
Create the object-storage bucket and credentials through your platform's storage process or Provider Storage. Provider Datalab reads an existing input Secret with the same name as the Datalab.

The Secret must exist in storage.secretNamespace and contain AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY. The storage identity must permit bucket listing with s3:ListAllMyBuckets. The endpoint must support path-style S3 requests.

The registry needs a bucket with the same name as the Datalab and permission to read, write, list, delete, and use multipart uploads. Distribution uses its standard object layout without an extra prefix or PVC. Disabling the registry retains its S3 objects. Set defaults.registry.enabled: false when the platform does not provide this storage.

For a manual setup, create the Secret with your credential values:

kubectl -n datalab create secret generic s-joe \
  --from-literal=AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID='<KEY_ID>' \
  --from-literal=AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY='<SECRET>'

Use the platform's Secret tools for shared installations. Keep live credentials out of Git.

docs.title: 6. Create a Datalab
docs.text:
Save this resource as datalab.yaml. The user joe must already exist in Keycloak. This uses the Joe example with an explicit claim namespace.

apiVersion: pkg.internal/v1beta2
kind: Datalab
metadata:
  name: s-joe
  namespace: workspace
spec:
  users:
  - joe

Apply it and check its conditions:

kubectl apply -f datalab.yaml
kubectl get datalabs -n workspace
kubectl describe datalab s-joe -n workspace

See Use a Datalab for session state, managed services, workshop files, and sharing.

docs.title: 7. Check the installation
docs.text:
Check that provider and function revisions are healthy and that the Datalab reports Synced=True and Ready=True:

kubectl get providers.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get providerrevisions.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get functions.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get functionrevisions.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get configurations.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get configurationrevisions.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get datalabs -n workspace

If reconciliation fails, read the Datalab conditions and events. Check that the required APIs are served. The provider APIs used here are namespaced:

kubectl api-resources --api-group=kubernetes.m.crossplane.io
kubectl api-resources --api-group=helm.m.crossplane.io
kubectl api-resources --api-group=keycloak.m.crossplane.io
kubectl api-resources --api-group=gateway.networking.k8s.io

For a managed store, also check its API group from the prerequisite table. Verify the Data address, storage access, and each requested service. If you declared a session, also check its browser login before giving users access.

docs.title: S3 client access
docs.text: The read-only S3 endpoint is experimental. Range reads currently return HTTP 200 with Content-Range, rather than HTTP 206.

docs.title: Enable the endpoint
docs.text:
Set httpRoute.enableS3: true in the selected EnvironmentConfig, with Gateway Data exposure configured under Service addresses. This adds the S3 endpoint to each Data-enabled Datalab's browser hostname.

Use a Gateway API controller that supports HTTPRoute header regular expressions, such as Contour. Add a ReferenceGrant if its certificate Secret is in another namespace. With S3 disabled, Data requests use the browser service. The network policies must permit access from the Gateway and access to object storage and IAM.

docs.title: S3 access to s-jane
docs.text:
The Jane example creates the Datalab s-jane and selects datalab-custom. With the example EnvironmentConfig, its endpoint is https://s-jane.lab.acme.com and its issuer is https://identity.acme.com/realms/acme. Replace these example DNS names with your environment's values.

Keycloak checks CLIENT_SECRET and issues a JWT. The AWS CLI sends it as AWS_SESSION_TOKEN in the X-Amz-Security-Token header. NGINX checks the tenant ID and passes the token to oauth2-proxy, which checks its signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and Datalab role. After authorization, rclone serve s3 checks the original AWS SigV4 request using s-jane as both signing values. It serves read-only data through separate upstream storage credentials.

Credential field Value AccessKeyId s-jane SecretAccessKey s-jane SessionToken Keycloak JWT access token Expiration Token expiry

The signing values are public tenant identifiers. They do not grant access without a valid JWT. The token must include s-jane in aud and at least one of ws_access, ws_admin, or ws_api under resource_access.s-jane.roles. These are Keycloak client roles, separate from OAuth scopes. All three permit reads. The upstream storage policy limits which buckets and objects the Datalab can read. Missing or invalid tokens cannot use a browser cookie or an unsigned request as a fallback.

The generated Datalab client always adds its own audience. Other OAuth clients must emit the same audience and tenant roles. Service-account tokens do not need a verified email address.

The following Bash commands use the credential helper from the repository root. It uses the client credentials grant with s-jane as the client ID. At the prompt, enter clientSecret from the Secret referenced by the client's status.oauth2[].secretRef. The commands read bucket s-jane with path-style requests. Change the bucket name if your storage uses another name.

Set the client secret for either method:

CLIENT_SECRET="$(python3 -c 'import getpass; print(getpass.getpass("CLIENT_SECRET: "))')"
export CLIENT_SECRET

docs.title: Manual token retrieval
docs.text:
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=s-jane AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=s-jane
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=https://s-jane.lab.acme.com
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1
export AWS_PROFILE=s-jane
aws configure set s3.addressing_style path --profile s-jane

credentials="$(python3 tests/s3/s3-credentials.py \
  --tenant s-jane \
  --issuer https://identity.acme.com/realms/acme)"
AWS_SESSION_TOKEN="$(printf '%s' "$credentials" | \
  python3 -c 'import json, sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["SessionToken"])')"
export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN
unset credentials

aws s3 ls s3://s-jane/

Run the token retrieval command again after the token expires, or use automatic renewal below.

docs.title: Automatic token renewal with credential_process
docs.text:
Clear the manual AWS settings so that the CLI uses the profile's credential process. The CLI obtains new credentials when needed, using the helper's Expiration value.

unset AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN
unset AWS_CONFIG_FILE AWS_PROFILE AWS_ENDPOINT_URL
unset AWS_DEFAULT_REGION AWS_REGION

export AWS_PROFILE=s-jane

aws configure set region us-east-1 --profile s-jane
aws configure set endpoint_url https://s-jane.lab.acme.com --profile s-jane
aws configure set s3.addressing_style path --profile s-jane
aws configure set credential_process \
  "python3 \"$PWD/tests/s3/s3-credentials.py\" --tenant s-jane --issuer https://identity.acme.com/realms/acme" \
  --profile s-jane

aws s3 ls s3://s-jane/

Keep CLIENT_SECRET available in the environment of the AWS CLI or SDK process. If you move the repository, update the helper's absolute path in the profile.

The endpoint supports list, HEAD, GET, and byte-range GET requests. It remains read only even when the Data browser has write permissions. Writes and presigned S3 URLs are rejected. packageR download and share links use the browser route.

docs.title: Use a Datalab
docs.text: A Datalab resource defines the users, sessions, and services for a team. The operator supplies the shared storage, identity, and network settings. Complete installation before applying these examples.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
A session is a named workspace with an editor, terminal, and persistent home directory. Declare the sessions you need in spec.sessions:

spec:
  sessions:
  - name: default
  - name: analysis
    state: stopped

The state defaults to started. A started session has a workspace Pod. A stopped session keeps its PVC without a running workspace. Change its state to started to use the same PVC again. Several sessions can run at once; each has its own Pod and PVC and shares the Datalab's credentials and managed services.

With no declared sessions, the Datalab still creates its shared services. It creates no session Pods or workspace PVCs.

status.sessions is a list keyed by name:

status:
  sessions:
  - name: default
    state: started
    phase: Running
    pvcSize: "1Gi"
    pvcRef:
      name: s-jane-default-persistent
      namespace: s-jane
    url: https://s-jane-default.lab.acme.com

state reports the desired lifecycle. phase and optional message report observed runtime details. The URL is present only when the runtime is Running. Stopped sessions keep pvcRef but have no runtime details or URL. The reference identifies the target PVC; it does not report PVC readiness. pvcSize reports the requested capacity of the session PVC, including while stopped.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text: Each declared session has a PVC mounted at /home/eduk8s. Its size and StorageClass come from the selected EnvironmentConfig. Use this volume for code, libraries, and workspace files. Keep datasets in object storage and database records in a managed database. Arrange backup and recovery with the operator.

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text:
Use spec.databases to request a PostgreSQL cluster and its logical databases:

spec:
  databases:
    pg0:
      names:
      - dev
      - prod
      storage: 1Gi
      backupStorage: 3Gi

This creates the pg0 cluster with dev and prod databases. The PostgreSQL operator manages the database Pods, credentials, and configured backups. Stopping a session does not stop the database.

Sessions receive connection settings such as POSTGRES_PG0_HOST, POSTGRES_PG0_PORT, and POSTGRES_PG0_DEV_URL. The generated <datalab>-datalab Secret holds these values. When the platform enables an external TLSRoute, it also supplies POSTGRES_PG0_DEV_URL_EXTERNAL. External connections require a client that supports direct TLS with SNI.

docs.title: Connect from a session
docs.text:
Use the connection variables supplied to the session, such as POSTGRES_PG0_DEV_URL. The PostgreSQL operator also creates user Secrets named *-pguser-*. Use the database role assigned to your task; the postgres role has administrative access.

See Additional services for a psql example.

docs.title: MongoDB and Redis
docs.text:
Use these fields to request MongoDB and Redis stores:

spec:
  documentStores:
    prod:
      storage: 1Gi
      backupStorage: 3Gi
  cacheStores:
    prod:
      storage: 1Gi
      backupStorage: 3Gi

Each store needs its operator installed in the cluster. For the name prod, sessions receive MONGO_PROD_URI and REDIS_PROD_URL, along with separate host and credential fields where available.

The composition creates <store>-mongodb-auth and <store>-redis-auth Secrets. It watches their values and copies connection settings into <datalab>-datalab. Sessions import those settings as environment variables. Restart a session to load changed values.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
Set backupStorage to a positive Kubernetes storage quantity, such as 10Gi, to create a separate backup PVC. Zero or an omitted value disables backups without stopping the store.

Store Backup schedule Retention PostgreSQL pgBackRest: full on Sunday, differential on other days, at 01:00 in the operator's time zone. Four full backups and their dependent backups; the volume also holds WAL. MongoDB Full mongodump --oplog --gzip archive daily at 01:00 UTC. Four completed archives. Redis Full redis-cli --rdb snapshot daily at 01:00 UTC, checked with redis-check-rdb. Four completed snapshots.

Size the volume for retained backups and the next full export. Monitor failed Jobs and free space. Failed MongoDB or Redis jobs preserve completed backups. Enabling or disabling Redis backups restarts its Pod.

docs.title: Data and sharing
docs.text:
The Data service, packageR, is a file browser for the Datalab's object storage. A session's Data tab opens this shared service. With a permanent Data address, you can also use it without a running session.

The file browser requires sign-in. Share individual files through temporary download URLs, or folders through public share links. Recipients do not need a Datalab account.

The operator controls service availability and read-only permissions through EnvironmentConfig. Storage IAM limits every request. For read-only access with AWS tools, see S3 client access.

docs.title: Sharing data with the world
docs.text:
Put files in <datalab>/public in the bucket named after your Datalab, then send the public share link. For example, s-jane/public/results.csv belongs to the default public share for s-jane. A folder named public elsewhere is not shared automatically.

Public sharing needs a permanent Data address. Upload files through the Data browser when write access is allowed, or use your storage tools. Anyone with the link can browse and download those files without signing in.

docs.title: OCI registry
docs.text:
The shared registry is available at https://s-jane.lab.acme.com/v2/ for Datalab s-jane. Use the registry connection named primary in status.connections to find its Secret. Enter that Secret's user and password at the Docker login prompt:

docker login s-jane.lab.acme.com
docker tag example:latest s-jane.lab.acme.com/team/example:latest
docker push s-jane.lab.acme.com/team/example:latest

Docker login and image references use the hostname without /v2/. Images use the Datalab's S3 bucket and remain available when sessions stop. The operator can disable the registry through the EnvironmentConfig.

docs.title: Files and the Workshop tab
docs.text:
The operator sets EnvironmentConfig.data.defaults.files to load workshop content from Git, an OCI image, or an HTTP archive. For example:

data:
  defaults:
    files:
    - git:
        url: https://github.com/versioneer-tech/datalab-example
        ref: origin/main
      includePaths:
      - /workshop/**
      path: .

Adding a source enables the Workshop tab. With no sources, the tab is hidden. Use includePaths, excludePaths, newRootPath, and path to select and place the files.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The named users must exist in Keycloak and their storage Secrets must exist before you apply these manifests in your claim namespace.

Manifest Environment Use Joe datalab Data without a session. Jeff, Jim, and Jane datalab Shared PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis stores; Jim has the Datalab admin role. Jane datalab-custom A virtual cluster with service Secret bindings, PostgreSQL, and a started session. John datalab-custom Started and stopped sessions with workshop files.

The environment examples show the two configurations. datalab-custom demonstrates read-only Data, custom quotas and StorageClasses, privileged security with the Kubernetes admin role, vCluster, registry, file bundles, Gateway and S3 access, and internal network rules. Adapt these settings to your platform's access policy.

docs.title: Check provisioning
docs.text:
Check the Datalab conditions after applying a resource:

kubectl get datalabs -n workspace
kubectl describe datalab s-jeff -n workspace

Synced=True means the composition reconciled. Ready=True means its resources report ready. Read the conditions and events if either is false. Session names, state, phase, messages, PVC references, and URLs are in status.sessions. Service connections and public virtual API profiles are in status.connections. Read each connection through its secretRef.

For connection fields and readiness, see the API reference. OAuth2 discovery lists the Datalab client separately in status.oauth2.

docs.title: Use a Datalab virtual cluster
docs.text:
Declare each virtual Kubernetes cluster under spec.vclusters:

apiVersion: pkg.internal/v1beta2
kind: Datalab
metadata:
  name: s-joe
  namespace: workspace
spec:
  users: [joe]
  vclusters:
    vc0:
      storage: 5Gi
      groups:
      - name: namespace-demo
        namespace: demo
        role: edit

Each entry creates one runtime in status.runtimeNamespace. Add vc1 alongside vc0 to create another cluster. An empty map creates none. Sessions and their environment-controlled vclusters remain separate.

docs.title: API access
docs.text:
The virtual API for vc0 is:

https://s-joe.lab.acme.com/.vc0

The Gateway removes /.vc0 and forwards to that instance with backend TLS validation. Workload Ingress and Gateway synchronization is disabled; use Kubernetes port forwarding to reach a workload Service.

docs.title: Roles and profiles
docs.text:
The API validates issuer, Datalab audience, signature, expiry, and configured roles under resource_access.<datalab>.roles. Kubernetes RBAC controls which operations those roles permit.

Caller Virtual API access A user in spec.users Explicit additional profiles, through the Datalab users group A Datalab administrator Additional profiles and each instance's built-in vcluster_<instance>_cluster-admin role The Datalab service account None by default; its only default role is ws_api An identity with an assigned vcluster_<instance>_<group> role The group's configured namespace and Kubernetes role

groups defines additional profiles with view, edit, or admin access. The provider grants their client roles to both Datalab groups. Optional OAuth scopes select which assigned roles appear in Datalab client tokens. Roles are specific to an instance. See token exchange for a token limited to one selected profile.

A downloaded profile selects the endpoint and default namespace. It neither grants access nor reduces permissions already present in the caller's token. The cluster-admin profile cannot elevate a namespace caller, and a namespace profile cannot restrict a caller who already has the admin role.

Provider Datalab already assigns workspace administrators ws_admin and each instance's vcluster_<instance>_cluster-admin role through the managed administrators group. No additional manual role assignment is needed. The API checks the instance role in the token. An unrelated manual assignment of ws_admin alone does not grant virtual API access.

docs.title: Download a profile
docs.text:
Resolve its Secret reference from status.connections; do not construct the name. Each profile Secret contains kubeconfig, the Datalab client's public client-id, and issuer-url. Public CA certificates can be included. It contains no client secret, token, private key, or client certificate. The provider keeps the recovery kubeconfig private.

ready: true reports runtime, routing, role, scope, and RBAC readiness. It does not imply caller authorization or require caller credentials to be present. The kubeconfig includes a Python 3 credential helper. Additional profiles select --token-only and read an access token file supplied by the caller. They require no OAuth client ID or client secret and make no token requests. The built-in cluster-admin profile retains the Datalab client ID and issuer. It accepts a caller token or a separate client secret for device login as a user. It never requests a service-account token. No separate helper file is needed on the caller's machine.

The following cases use Datalab s-joe, instance vc0, and the additional namespace-demo profile from the example above. Use Bash with kubectl, jq, base64, and Python 3 installed. Set the host context used to read Datalab metadata and download Secrets:

set -euo pipefail
umask 077
host_context=your-host-context

Replace your-host-context with the platform context. Download commands use that context explicitly. Commands with --kubeconfig connect to the virtual cluster. If you cannot read the host Datalab or its Secrets, obtain the files from the platform operator and continue with the local steps.

Case Local kubeconfig file Credential supplied by the caller Human device login s-joe-vc0.kubeconfig Datalab OAuth client secret; browser login identifies the user Delegated access s-joe-vcluster-vc0_namespace-demo.kubeconfig An exchanged user access token for the selected profile

These are local filenames. Always resolve the host Secret names and namespaces from Datalab status. The download commands require a ready profile.

docs.title: Human access
docs.text: This case logs in as your Keycloak user. The client secret authenticates the Datalab client; your user identity and assigned roles control API access.

docs.title: 1. Download the profile with device login
docs.text:
Select the built-in cluster-admin profile. Its helper supports device login even when your user has only an additional namespace role.

read -r profile_namespace profile_secret < <(
  kubectl --context "${host_context}" -n workspace get datalab s-joe -o json | \
    jq -er '.status.connections[] |
      select(.type == "vcluster" and .instance == "vc0" and
             .group == "cluster-admin" and .ready == true) |
      .secretRef | [.namespace, .name] | @tsv'
)
kubectl --context "${host_context}" -n "${profile_namespace}" \
  get secret "${profile_secret}" -o jsonpath='{.data.kubeconfig}' | \
  base64 --decode > s-joe-vc0.kubeconfig

docs.title: 2. Download the OAuth client secret
docs.text:
Resolve the ready client credential reference from status.oauth2. Save only its decoded client secret value in a private file. The helper does not read a Secret YAML document.

unset DATALAB_ACCESS_TOKEN_FILE
mkdir -p "$HOME/.config/datalab"
chmod 700 "$HOME/.config/datalab"
export DATALAB_CLIENT_SECRET_FILE="$HOME/.config/datalab/s-joe-client-secret"
read -r oauth_namespace oauth_secret < <(
  kubectl --context "${host_context}" -n workspace get datalab s-joe -o json | \
    jq -er '.status.oauth2[] |
      select(.type == "client" and .ready == true) |
      .secretRef | [.namespace, .name] | @tsv'
)
kubectl --context "${host_context}" -n "${oauth_namespace}" \
  get secret "${oauth_secret}" -o json | \
  jq -er '.data.clientSecret // .data.client_secret' | \
  base64 --decode > "$DATALAB_CLIENT_SECRET_FILE"
chmod 600 "$DATALAB_CLIENT_SECRET_FILE"

You can instead obtain that value through the platform's credential process. If DATALAB_CLIENT_SECRET_FILE is unset, the helper asks for the secret in an interactive terminal without showing or saving the input. A valid cached access token needs no secret. Refresh and new login need the secret again.

docs.title: 3. Start kubectl and approve the device login
docs.text:
For a user with vcluster_vc0_cluster-admin, run:

kubectl --kubeconfig ./s-joe-vc0.kubeconfig get namespaces
kubectl --kubeconfig ./s-joe-vc0.kubeconfig auth can-i '*' '*' --all-namespaces

On the first command, the helper prints a verification URL and a user code. Open the URL in a browser, enter the code, and sign in as your Keycloak user. The browser can run on another device. After approval, kubectl continues. The authorization check returns yes for a user whose token contains the built-in administrator role and whose binding is ready.
